source.title: Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The study measures self-repair and attributes some of it to LayerNorm scaling and MLP-neuron Anti-Erasure, but does not test Copy Suppression itself or compare its contribution with these mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on general self-repair mechanisms. Its statements about Copy Suppression are descriptions of prior work, not results from this study. It does not report a test of GPT-2 Small L10H7's copy-suppression role, its weights-based circuit, calibration, or the specific upstream-copier ablation described in V4.
record.test_reason: The study measures self-repair of individual attention heads across the Pile in GPT-2 and Pythia models. It attributes a share of that self-repair to sources other than copy suppression: LayerNorm scaling (about 30% of direct effect) and sparse MLP Anti-Erasure neurons. This bears on V6's claim that self-repair across the distribution comes mainly from other mechanisms. The study never measures copy suppression's own share, and its statements about L10H7 and copy suppression only cite prior work (McDougall et al.).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that head self-repair exists across the pretraining distribution and models, but is imperfect and noisy. LayerNorm scaling (around 30%) and sparse neuron Anti-Erasure contribute to it. They add that LayerNorm explains only up to ~30%, that other mechanisms remain, and that some self-repair may be an off-distribution side effect of ablation. They do not quantify copy suppression's share.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses resample ablation and direct-effect/logit measurements to investigate self-repair mechanisms across models. It does not reproduce the original Copy Suppression circuit analysis or measure its 76.9% loss attribution.
record.method_sensitivity: The LayerNorm estimate depends on selecting the top 2% of tokens by direct effect and clipping per-token percentages between 0 and 100%; the authors state that these choices materially affect the estimate. Self-repair also varies substantially across tokens and heads.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-repair of individual heads exists across the full Pile distribution in many models. It is imperfect and noisy, sometimes overcorrecting (Figures 1–3, 20–22).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Self-repair of individual attention heads is general across the pretraining distribution but incomplete and highly token-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-repressing heads: GPT2-Medium L21H1's direct effect drops in proportion to how much of its own output is added back to its input (Figure 9, 19).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some heads suppress their own contribution when their signal is already present, a suppression motif distinct from copy suppression.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: The LayerNorm estimate is explicitly described as directional rather than precise and depends on filtering and clipping. Self-repair is noisy across prompts and heads. The study does not compare the contribution of Copy Suppression with LayerNorm or Anti-Erasure.

untested.parts: All: L10H7's suppression role in GPT-2 Small is only cited from prior work.
All: no QK/OV circuit analysis or loss attribution.
All: no upstream-copier ablation with a copy suppression head measured; the copy-suppression Anti-Erasure motif is cited from McDougall et al.
All: IOI backup/negative name movers are discussed but not tested as copy suppression.
Copy suppression's own share of self-repair, and whether all other sources together form the majority, are not measured.

missing.what: Appendix C: about 60% of final-layer neurons show negligible change and 40% show small, cancelling changes. Sparse Anti-Erasure is therefore one MLP mechanism among others.
Anecdotal claim that a few top self-repairing neurons often sum to the vast majority of the layer's self-repair.
Ratio of clean to ablated LayerNorm scale exceeds 1 on 90.66% of tokens (resample), 98.75% (mean) and 100% (zero) for Pythia-160M L11H2.

record.verdict_notes: Co-author Rushing is also an author of the original copy suppression paper, but this study is not an original source. The reader's limits_scope label rested on metric caveats and untested parts, which are not grounds for limits_scope under the rules. It is replaced with a narrow 'supports' label on R1 only. Anti-Erasure here occurs in MLP neurons, not heads, so it counts as an 'other mechanism' for V6.

versions.untested_parts: Whether GPT-2 Small L10H7 suppresses context-present tokens predicted by earlier components, or has that main role across the training distribution.
The QK and OV circuits of GPT-2 Small L10H7 and whether they explain 76.9% of its effect on loss.
Whether Copy Suppression improves calibration by reducing overconfidence in naive copying.
Whether ablating an upstream copier reduces suppression and thereby partly compensates for the ablation.
Whether negative heads in narrow tasks or other models and sizes share the Copy Suppression role.
The study measures LayerNorm and Anti-Erasure contributions to self-repair, but does not measure Copy Suppression's contribution or establish that it is small relative to other mechanisms.

rows.subject: multiple models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Pythia suite, GPT2-Small, GPT2-Medium, and GPT2-Large
rows.operation_detail: Resample ablated individual attention heads and estimated the LayerNorm contribution to self-repair.

conditions.value: percentages capped between 0 and 100%; averaged across many layers

rows.measure: LayerNorm self-repair as a fraction of the ablated head's clean direct effect
rows.value: around 30% of the direct effect of a head on average across many layers
rows.note: The authors describe this as a directional metric rather than a precise estimate; clipping and filtering affect the result. It quantifies one mechanism, not its contribution relative to Copy Suppression.
rows.check: The value is a capped (0–100%), top-2%-filtered directional statistic read from Figure 11. It shows LayerNorm, a non-copy-suppression source, accounts for a nontrivial share (~30%), but not a majority. Copy suppression's share is not measured. 'Partial' is right for the 'mainly other sources' claim.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V6. LayerNorm accounts for approximately 30% of head direct effect under filtering and clipping; neither the majority contribution of other mechanisms nor copy suppression's small share is measured.
source_check.problem: A nontrivial LayerNorm contribution does not establish even a quantitatively partial result on V6's comparative claim.

rows.subject: pythia-160m
rows.operation_detail: Resample ablated L10H11 and measured changes in the final MLP layer's neuron direct effects.

conditions.value: selected for strong self-repair by the last MLP layer

rows.measure: Clean and ablated direct effects of the top self-repairing neuron
rows.value: The top self-repairing neuron commonly had a negative clean direct effect and a less negative ablated direct effect.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as a neuron reducing its Erasure after the head is ablated. This selected-token example does not quantify the mechanism's share of total self-repair or compare it with Copy Suppression.
rows.check: Qualitative example on tokens selected for strong MLP self-repair; shows Anti-Erasure exists in a non-copy-suppression component but gives no share of total self-repair.

rows.subject: Llama-7b
rows.operation_detail: Resample ablated L30H8 and measured self-repair by neurons in the final MLP layer.
rows.measure: Frequency with which the top self-repairing neuron compensates for a share of the head's direct effect
rows.value: The top self-repairing neuron repairs 10% of the direct effect in over 40% of instances.
rows.note: This is an example of neuron-level Anti-Erasure, not a measure of its share of total self-repair or of Copy Suppression's share.
rows.check: Llama-7B neuron frequency statistic; shows sparse neuron Anti-Erasure but not its share of total self-repair versus copy suppression.

relationships.condition: Individual-head resample ablations on top-2% direct-effect tokens of The Pile; GPT-2 S/M/L and Pythia 160M–1B
relationships.reason: LayerNorm scaling alone explains about 30% of a head's direct effect on average (R1). This is a substantial non-copy-suppression source, consistent with V6. The comparison with copy suppression's share is untested.
relationships.display_finding: LayerNorm scaling explained about 30% of a head’s direct effect on average; whether other mechanisms dominate self-repair or copy suppression contributes little remained untested.

source_check.condition: Individual-head resample ablations on top-2% direct-effect tokens of The Pile; GPT-2 S/M/L and Pythia 160M–1B
source_check.reason: R1 establishes a LayerNorm contribution relative to head direct effect, not that other mechanisms provide most self-repair or that copy suppression provides a small share. Those comparisons are untested; they justify neither supports nor limits_scope.

relation.reason: Its own interventions test the non-copy-suppression mechanisms named in V6, although they do not determine its comparative clauses.

tranche.reason: Extends self-repair mechanism measurements to individual-head ablations on general pretraining text across additional models.

source_check.notes: The approximately 30% denominator is head direct effect, not total self-repair; the paper sometimes uses looser wording elsewhere. Catalog-wide counts and claims about the original paper were not independently checked.

statements.correction: Section 3.2 and Appendix A: filtered, clipped LayerNorm/direct-effect averages center around 30% for most models on many layers; no pooled six-model statistic stated. Pack header explicitly flags two shared authors. Majority contribution and copy suppression's relative share unmeasured.
statements.problem: The approximately 30% observation is not reported as a pooled average across six models. The statement also incorrectly says the supplied header lacks an author-sharing flag. These results do not establish V6's comparative claim.

statements.correction: Section 3.2 analyzes individual attention heads across models. Figure 8's GPT-2 Small neuron experiment uses L9H11. No distribution-wide attribution compares copy suppression's share with LayerNorm and other mechanisms.
statements.problem: The missing comparative measurement is correctly identified, but the suggestion that this study ablates only heads other than L10H7 overgeneralizes the selected neuron experiments.

statements.correction: Section 2.2, Figure 2: averages across the whole sampled dataset. Appendix A, Figure 10: entire-distribution averages without clipping. Figure 11: filtered and clipped statistic underlying the approximately 30% observation. Comparative V6 attribution remains unmeasured.
statements.problem: The top-2% selection and clipping describe the approximately 30% estimate, but the paper also reports unselected analyses.

statements.correction: Pythia-1B appears in Figures 1–2, 6 and 10–11. Llama-7B appears in the neuron-frequency experiment. Models above approximately 7B and instruct/chat stages are not tested.
statements.problem: Llama-7B is not the study's only model in the stated 1–10B range; Pythia-1B also has self-repair and LayerNorm results.

statements.correction: Section 2.2 and Figure 2 report whole-dataset averages; Appendix A and Figure 10 report entire-distribution LayerNorm ratios without clipping. The directional approximately 30% statistic uses filtering and clipping.
statements.problem: The approximately 30% estimate is filtered, but the assertion that this study never uses an unselected sample is false.

statements.correction: Sections 2.1 and 3.2 measure direct-effect self-repair and decompose it into downstream heads, MLPs and LayerNorm. Section 4 examines selected heads and neurons. No joint measurement attributes self-repair to L10H7-mediated copy suppression versus these mechanisms.
statements.problem: The differing measurements and missing joint attribution are correctly identified. The paper does not establish that none of the ablated heads is an upstream copier suppressed by L10H7.

statements.correction: R1 state=cannot_determine for V6. LayerNorm and sparse neuronal Anti-Erasure are demonstrated; majority contribution and copy suppression's small share are unmeasured. Figure 8 uses GPT-2 Small L9H11; Section 3.2 analyzes individual heads across models.
statements.problem: The empirical summary is largely accurate, but R1 cannot determine V6's comparative claim. L9H11 identifies the selected neuron experiment, not the full GPT-2 Small ablation analysis.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: LayerNorm attribution and selected Anti-Erasure analyses
reader_labels.reason: LayerNorm is estimated to account for around 30% using a capped, directional statistic, while the neuron analyses are selected examples and do not quantify overall mechanism shares or Copy Suppression's contribution (R1-R12).
